pr_body:
Closes https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/7396

Stuff that this PR adds/changes:
1. `HeadOptions` for the head block to cut down on arguments for `NewHead()`
2. `SetMinValidTime` method for Head.
3. `MinValidTimeGracePeriod` as described in the linked issue. 
4. Updates the head compaction logic.
5. Adds `prometheus_tsdb_head_compactions_triggered_total` to know exactly how many times the head compaction was triggered.

TODO:
- [x] Unit tests
- [ ] Test it in Cortex to find any issues

issue_context.title: Configurable minValidTime in the head block
issue_context.body:
## Introduction 

Head block has a concept of `minValidTime` wherein it won't allow samples before 1h to be ingested (Called out of bound samples)

## Proposal

Here I propose making `minValidTime` configurable which is solely for external users of TSDB and does not affect the functioning of Prometheus.

Sometimes we want to ingest some old data because of long outages lasting >1h. In such cases, the `minValidTime` is a blocker. Making it configurable will allow ingesting old data.

Out of order samples are still discarded.

## Changes required

**To configure `minValidTime`**

There are 2 possible ways we could make it configurable.

1. Introduce a method `SetMinValidTime()` which will set it to the value passed. But this one is easy to make mistakes.

2. Pass a config, let's say `MinValidTimeGracePeriod`, which will accept samples up to `MinValidTimeGracePeriod` back in time from the current `minValidTime` that we calculate.

**To the compaction**

Allowing old samples can interfere with head compaction. So the compaction check for Head can be changed 
from `head.maxt - head.mint >= chunkRange * 3/2`
to `if len(blocks) > 0 { head.maxt - lastBlock.maxt >= chunkRange * 3/2 } else { old condition }`

Vertical compaction and vertical queries needs to be enabled to take care of overlapping data.

## Is it safe

Memory: It is proportional to the number of series. With m-mapping in place, taking in lots of old samples is not a problem.

Data: The vertical query and vertical compaction take care of everything. The user must be aware of what they are getting into.

cc @JessicaGreben

Uhm, don't we already have this setting via the min block size?

I'm also unclear how this would actually work, as we've already written out the blocks for older data by then.
Vertical compaction would handle those newly created ones

> Uhm, don't we already have this setting via the min block size?

The idea is to keep the block size same as before and allow old samples in case needed in certain scenarios.
That sounds amazing for #535 too
Yes, this is an amazing step forward in to backfillable Remote Write :+1:

This might not help much for #535 as we need to align the data with existing blocks to avoid large blocks. But backfillable Remote Write, definitely.

While using configurable minValidTime, the compaction planner needs to be a little different else it is possible to create very large blocks with carefully planned samples. Hence I don't see this being exposed to users of Prometheus.
And can't we somehow combine both usecases in one solution ? Maybe this proposal can be adapted...
Well "backfillable Remote Write" might be the answer to #535

This PR that we plan to do does not solve all problems of full  https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/535 - however it's a good first step. I would focus on "short term backfill capabilities" and then we are already planning with @codesome and @pracucci to think about some compaction planner / logic to fix the large blocks problem that has to be solved for https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/535

Let's focus on this first step only for now I think :hugs:
I will open a PR for making `minValidTime` configurable.

This doesn't solve #535 at all, it's more a way to do push than one-off backfilling of old data.

How would you preserve the property that Prometheus time series are append-only? Right now the only place we check for that is in the head.

> How would you preserve the property that Prometheus time series are append-only?

In the context of Prometheus, that would be done by setting the grace period to 0. But for external users who would set it to >0, it is difficult to assure that efficiently, it will need a lookup into the blocks. This is an issue for series which disappear in between or super long scrape intervals (like, in hours). Otherwise, there would be at least 1 sample of the series in the Head which will make old samples out of order.

Also, if data like this is continously being ingested wouldn't it create a pile of tiny chunks due to the continuous head compactions?

If this is just a thing that affects Cortex, it may be better for Cortex to have a 2nd head for the older data.

This is same for Thanos.

Plus we can compact chunks if needed on compactor.

> Also, if data like this is continously being ingested wouldn't it create a pile of tiny chunks due to the continuous head compactions?

Compaction as Bartek said. Maybe we can revive https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/6332 :)

> If this is just a thing that affects Cortex, it may be better for Cortex to have a 2nd head for the older data.

This idea is also into consideration. But allowing older samples in the existing TSDB instance is a much simpler solution than handling another head. So, that idea has been kept for explicit backfilling for now and this solution mainly aims to take care of some unexpected issues that might arise lasting longer than 1h.
Keep in mind that things have been optimised with the assumption that there's at most going to be tens of blocks. Suddenly having hundreds probably won't end too well.

> Suddenly having hundreds probably won't end too well.

In what case is that possible right now? (except for data spanning a LOT of years)
There are 120 minutes in a recent block, compaction is attempted every minute, thus you could have 120 tiny blocks with this change.

I have proposed a change in the compaction condition in the issue description which will avoid this :), it is also tested in the unit tests in the linked PR https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/7398

Hmm, I think that logic is right but the level of intricacies this proposal is adding make me uncomfortable. I think you could get the same net effect by increasing the block size in Cortex, without having to change any logic.

Increased restart times is the main concern for increasing the block size.

That said, I see only 2 main additions in the logic (1) Allow a bit older samples, which includes just looking back a bit more than minValidTime (2) Look at maxt of the last block instead of mint of the head during compaction if blocks exist. These 2 seem to be simple changes (I might be biased).

> Increased restart times is the main concern for increasing the block size.

Isn't that going to happen anyway with this change? Aren't restarts rare anyway?

> That said, I see only 2 main additions in the logic 

Ignoring the unrelated refactoring, it's also touching the WAL loading. More importantly it now requires quite a bit more thought around how compaction works.

> Isn't that going to happen anyway with this change?

This change is to allow samples a little older in time in case something goes wrong, and it does not necessarily increase the block size of every new block. In the majority of cases, it is still 2h blocks. So the restarts will remain same except for those cases where we end up ingesting old data.

> Aren't restarts rare anyway?

If you are talking about Cortex/Thanos - it's all during rollouts. So if you do weekly rollouts, then it's not rare, and usually, there are 10s of components using TSDB which would have 100s of TSDBs combined.

> it's also touching the WAL loading

Only for checking the min valid time, yes.

> More importantly it now requires quite a bit more thought around how compaction works.

Yes. This could be documented in the code at relevant places.

> In the majority of cases, it is still 2h blocks

You always have to presume a worst case when it comes to provisioning, and I'd presume by default that any feature like this will be abused and/or some system in a failing state will continuously push older data. So in terms of resource usage at least, things would have to be treated the same as though you had increased the block size. Similarly given that worst case, restarts will be as slow as if you had increased the block size.

> Yes. This could be documented in the code at relevant places.

That doesn't really address my point. My point is that these implications were not immediately obvious as they're emergent properties, and compound onto the existing complexity of the system and ultimately increase the likelihood of bugs, undesired interactions, and thus make future changes harder. Documenting the additional complexity that we've found so far doesn't change that there's now more complexity (likely including some we've yet to realise).

> You always have to presume a worst case when it comes to provisioning

> Similarly given that worst case, restarts will be as slow as if you had increased the block size.

Provisioning, agree, need to consider the worst case. But we cannot consider only the worst case for the restarts. If it was increasing the block size, then restarts are slower 100% of the time. With this minValidTime extension, the restarts are slower in failure cases where old data is pushed back. If the system (assuming the consumers of this feature to be Cortex and Thanos) provides reliable functioning 99% of the time, then its <1% times for the slow restarts (also, the TSDB need not restart when it's taking the old data, the WAL will get truncated eventually before a restart, so the slower restarts are even less).

A Prometheus cannot abuse this as this is not planned to be configurable in Prometheus binary and will be set to 0. 

> That doesn't really address my point. My point is that these implications were not immediately obvious as they're emergent properties, and compound onto the existing complexity of the system and ultimately increase the likelihood of bugs, undesired interactions, and thus make future changes harder. Documenting the additional complexity that we've found so far doesn't change that there's now more complexity (likely including some we've yet to realise).

I am open to spending more time investigating all implications because increasing block size is not a direct replacement for this for its current use cases.

So, here are couple of places where complexity adds up:

1.

The compaction logic needs a small change, which is, when there is at least 1 block on disk, consider the maxt of the last block for the compactable range instead of the head mint, as mint is affected by the grace period. 

This one is a small change and easy to understand.

2.

The main complexity is on the WAL replay side. During ingestion of samples, min valid time is not fixed, rather it is 1h before the maxt of head (hence it's a variable min valid time).

Currently during WAL replay, the min valid time is fixed to the maxt of the last block. But when there is a grace period, it cannot be fixed else it will cause unnecessary samples to be loaded from WAL which is alredy in the block.

Though WAL truncation happens to remove samples from the block, it cannot be 100% assured that all samples from the block are removed from the WAL.

After giving some thought, I realized that even if we are doing dynamic min valid time (with grace period) with the WAL replay, we are anyway going to load samples from WAL which are already in the block - because with the grace period, we have to look back from the maxt of the last block. So, after a restart, the head block is always going to overlap with the last block (unless WAL has got rid of all the samples not in the head).

This needs some more thought on how we want to handle it.

So, point 2 above is unavoidable, i.e., possible overlapping blocks after restart even if there was no sample in the grace period. I don't see how it can be tackled without an inefficient lookup in the blocks for many samples (or) modification in the WAL record (out of scope for this). So I think this trade-off is something we have to live with if we want configurable min valid time. @brian-brazil @bwplotka
That'd be quite inefficient and relatively complex for something Prometheus itself doesn't need, I'd suggest going with a larger block  size or having a 2nd head inside Cortex.
Another thought I just had is that we technically should probably be doing that check on every new series - not just at WAL replay.
Could you elaborate a bit?

Per above a known issue with this approach would be that it head block can contain samples which overlap with what's in the block, including out-of-order appends. The WAL issue is basically the same issue. I'm suggesting that anything done for one case should also be done for the other. This is all however quite a bit of complexity, as the head would no longer be a standalone block as it'd have to be coupled to the DB to do such checks.

> This is all however quite a bit of complexity, as the head would no longer be a standalone block as it'd have to be coupled to the DB to do such checks.

Yes. One of the directions could be to assure WAL never has samples from the blocks while we checkpoint, which means no unnecessary overlap on replay. But that is hard too.
Checkpoints only contain series, not samples - and we only read samples from after the last checkpoint anyway. The issue is that whether via scrape or WAL, there's samples overlapping with blocks.

Checkpoints can contain samples, but I was conveying something else.

Regarding overlap with blocks, yes, that is expected with current design during appending old samples and also replay. One of the other issues that I was first looking into was - _even if you don't have old samples in Head which overlap with the blocks, you can end up having overlapping samples after restart_, which can be solved if we assure after a Head Truncation no sample from blocks is present in the WAL.

Rewriting the entire WAL at each compaction doesn't strike me as something that'd be workable. Even then it wouldn't help. A sample could come in which overlaps with the blocks, Prometheus restarts, and there's an overlapping sample in the WAL which we shouldn't be discarding.
Right. No easy way to solve without re-write of many parts of TSDB. I am closing this now as there are hard to solve efficiently issues in this approach.

Thanks for this discussion. Definitely the replay is not easy. To me, we should maintain separate records for samples overlapping with the potential existing block so we know what to replay. Is this really difficult to implement?

Otherwise, yes we should compare this with starting another head block as proposed initially.

Thanks @codesome for nice investigation!
Discussed this offline with @bwplotka. A separate record would be too invasive change and has its own issues. So we plan to design it with having multiple TSDBs which could be simpler to implement.

review_comments: Why not have it as a hard value? Having the value consistently set to 1h for Prometheus would probably avoid some confusion.

If with a hard value you mean a constant, there might not be a single value that satisfies all use cases for external users, so I think configurable is better. And I was thinking of this being 0 for Prometheus for now as we have a flag to change the block size (though hidden), and setting this to a fixed size means the data is no longer assured to be non-overlapping.
I mean that rather as relative to whatever the current min block time is, have it relative to the max block time.

I'm also strongly opposed to this being configurable for Prometheus - we already have enough problems with users messing with the min block size and trying to use Prometheus for push without forcing Cortex design decisions onto Prometheus.

Do you mean to say take in a multiplier and use min/max block time on that to get the grace period?

Having it >0 for Prometheus means that we need to enable vertical compaction always, so let it be 0 for Prometheus. This option is only exposed in the TSDB package but nowhere configurable from the Prometheus binary.
I'm suggesting that rather than the head taking in 1-3h old data in Prometheus depending on where it is in the compaction cycle, that it'd always be a consistent 1h.

I miss spoke in the issue description (fixed now). It is actually 1h old consistently for Prometheus. So with this grace period, it will be `1h + grace period` consistently.

The relevant piece of code which maintains that 1h: https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/7b24bb311631f4eaa5d794b849770f436fc75b5a/tsdb/head.go#L1015

Ah, I didn't realise that.

In that case does that do the right thing in terms of blocks/WAL given that this minValidTime isn't tied to them?

What do you mean by the right thing here? If you mean `1h + grace period` old for samples, then yes, it will be that. And during WAL replay, as we use the time passed in the `Head.Init` as the min valid time, we just allow upto that `mint - grace period` for samples.

If the source data is coming from a Prometheus's WAL then that will be aligned with the 2h of the compaction cycle. This PR as proposed however is aligned with the current time. So there's a mismatch there.
Nice catch. IIUC we want the out of bounds to be always 1h consistent. So I will fix it during replay to consider that.
(after the open discussions are concluded in https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/7396)
Hmm, that doesn't sound right if your goal is to handle delayed data from remote write as that's not 1h delayed - it goes back to the start of the head which is on the 2h cycle.

I might be confusing things here. Here is what I understand right now:

1. Configurable grace period and not a fixed grace period. So, samples can overlap blocks too.
2. During an append, currently, it's fixed to max 1h old sample w.r.t. current maxt. So, this makes it `1h + grace period`
3. During WAL replay, we take min valid time as the maxt of the last block throughout the replay. So, while applying the grace period, we should take the min valid time w.r.t. the maxt of head block so that we don't end up with samples which are already in the block.

That all sounds right, but that's not what I'm talking about.

Consider you have a normal Prometheus using remote write, which has remote write delayed for some reason and then restarts. It will start re-sending samples from the WAL based on where the head is.

Now that's going to Cortex with all this code, will that Cortex be able to ingest all the samples from that Prometheus's remote write and if so how much grace does it need to do so?

> Now that's going to Cortex with all this code, will that Cortex be able to ingest all the samples from that Prometheus's remote write and if so how much grace does it need to do so?

Cortex will have a limit too on how old samples can it take and can't get away from it. The grace period will be a decision that needs to be taken on how long do you want to allow. This configuration would just give some extra time to fix things and wont completely eliminate losing data.
